To 1×107 cell pellets, 1 ml of ice-cold 1 mg/ml Biotin-SS-Sulfo-OSu (DOJINDO) in PBS to suspend the pellets, followed by rotation at 4 °C for 30 min, washing twice with quench buffer [50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 0.1 mM EDTA, 150 mM NaCl], and washing twice with PBS. Next, 1% PFA/PBS was added to the cell surface-biotinylated cells, the cells were fixed at room temperature for 5 min, and 1 M glycine was added, followed by incubation at room temperature for 5 min. After two washes with PBS, the cells were suspended in PBS/0.1% BSA/0.05% Tween-20 and dispensed into 96-well Pierce™ NeutrAvidin™-Coated High-Capacity Plates, Clear, 8-Well Strip (Thermo Fisher Scientific), at 50 μl/well (≤10,000 cells). The wells were left overnight at 4 °C with slow shaking and then washed twice with PBS.

Immunostaining. Cells were permeabilized with 1% Triton X-100 in PBS for 20 min and blocked with Blocking One-P (Nacalai Tesque Inc.) for 20 min at room temperature. Then, 2 μg/ml primary antibody solution in 0.1× Blocking One-P/PBS (mix of two antibodies for sci-mtChIL-seq) was added to the wells, which were shaken slowly at 4 °C for 6 h. After three washes (5 min each at 4 °C) with PBS, 2 μg/ml sci-ChIL probe solution was added to 0.1× Blocking One-P and 0.5 M NaCl/PBS (for sci-mtChIL-seq, the sci-ChIL probe combination is shown in Supplementary Data 2), and the mixture was shaken slowly overnight at 4 °C.

ChIL reaction. Tn5 (90 ng of purified Tn5) in 1× Tn5 dialysis buffer (50 mM HEPES-KOH, pH 7.2, 0.1 M NaCl, 0.1 mM EDTA, 1 mM dithiothreitol, 0.1% Triton X-100, and 10% glycerol) was added to each well and incubated for 10 min at room temperature. The Tn5 transposase was produced in-house following a previously described protocol41. MEDS-B (10 μM, 0.1 μl/well) in 1× Tn5 dialysis buffer was then added and allowed to react for 1 h at room temperature. After three washes with PBS (5 min at RT), 1× TAPS-DMF buffer (10 mM TAPS-NaOH, pH 8.5, 5 mM MgCl2, and 10% N,N-dimethylformamide) was added and reacted at 37 °C for 1 h for the Tn5-mediated integration reaction. The reaction was then stopped with 50 mM EDTA at 50 °C for 30 min, the mixture was washed three times with PBS, and then a fill-in solution (200 U per well T4 DNA ligase, NEB, 1.5 U T4 DNA Polymerase, NEB, in 1× T4 DNA Ligase Reaction buffer, NEB) was added, followed by incubation at room temperature for 30 min. The reaction was stopped with 50 mM EDTA at 50 °C for 30 min, followed by washing three times with PBS. After the addition of Hoechst to the wells and nuclear staining of the cells, Accumax (Nacalai Tesque Inc., 17087-54) for SP2 cells or a solution of Accumax: Accutase (Nacalai Tesque Inc., 12679-54) = 1:3 for embryonic cells and NIH3T3 cells was added and allowed to settle for 10 min at room temperature. Additionally, 1 M DTT (Nacalai Tesque Inc.) was added, and allowed to react at 37 °C for 30 min to allow the cells to detach from the plate. The entire supernatant was collected in a 15 ml tube and centrifuged to precipitate the cells. Approximately half of the volume of the supernatant was removed, a final concentration of 0.1% Tween-20/2% BSA in PBS was added, and the cells were resuspended. Sorting was performed on a SONY SH800. Cell solution was filtered through a 40 μm filter before sorting, and Hoechst-positive cells were sorted to 25 cells/well in a 96-well plate containing IVT solution (2 U/μl per well; TOYOBO). IVT reactions were then incubated at 37 °C for 3 h. RNA samples were treated with DNase I (2.5 U per well; TaKaRa) for 30 min at 37 °C. The treated RNA samples were purified by adding 1.8× volume of Agencourt RNAClean XP beads (Beckman Coulter). They were then incubated with the beads for 5 min at room temperature, washed twice gently in 70% ethanol, and eluted in 7 μl of nuclease-free-water. Reverse transcription was carried out in accordance with the protocol of the SMART-Seq v4 Ultra Low Input RNA Kit (Clontech/Takara) with minor modifications, but all reagents were prepared separately. In each well of a 96-well plate, 7 μl of purified RNA were added in 1.4 μl of reaction buffer [0.655 μl of 10× Lysis Buffer, 0.7 μl of Read 2 primer (12 μM), 0.035 μl of RNase inhibitor]. Samples were incubated at 72 °C in a preheated, hot-lid thermal cycler for 3 min. Then, the samples were supplemented with 2.8 μl of 5× First-Strand Buffer, 1 μl of Advantage Ultra Pure PCR Deoxynucleotide Mix, 1 μl of DTT, 0.25 μl of RNase Inhibitor, and 1 μl of SMART Scribe Reverse Transcriptase. The reverse transcription was performed in a thermal cycler with the following program: Step 1: 42 °C × 90 min, followed by Step 2: 70 °C for 30 min and holding at 4 °C. Single-cell data analysis
Read mapping and processing. To obtain the sequences of both the reads and dual indices, run the following command: “bcl2fastq --create-fastq-for-index -R bclfile_directory.” Cell barcodes were made by modifying the index fastq files by seqkit (version 0.16.1)42. Cell barcodes were added to the read names using umi_tools (version 1.1.1)43. Adapter sequences were trimmed using TrimGalore (version 0.6.10) with the default options. Paired reads were mapped to mm10 by Bowtie2 (version 2.3.5.1)44 with the default options. BAM files were created, sorted, and indexed by SAMtools (version 1.18)45. Paired reads mapped to autosomes and sex chromosomes were obtained. To obtain unique reads, PCR duplicates that had the same cell barcode and were mapped to the same site were excluded. Unique reads with the same cell barcode and with the same start position are expected to be caused by random primers in IVT. Unique fragments were obtained by removing the reads. The number of obtained single-cell data and the average read counts per cell were provided in Supplementary Data 4.

Quality control. Out of the expected 96×96 barcodes, up to 2400 barcodes were assigned to a cell in the experimental design in this study. Therefore, barcodes with a low number of fragments, which were not assigned to any cell, and detected by chance. To exclude these barcodes, thresholds for the number of fragments were set for each dataset. To calculate appropriate thresholds, the distributions of the number of fragments for assigned and unassigned barcodes were estimated, respectively, using the EM algorithm implemented in the R package mixtools (v2.0.0)46. Thresholds were set when the cumulative probability of the assigned barcode distribution reached 0.01.

Additionally, to evaluate the risk of doublets (collisions of the cell barcodes) in the combinatorial indexing procedure, we created the n×m contingency table of the number of reads obtained X=(xij) for all combinations of primary (T5) and secondary index (i5+i7). We assumed that (a) the first stage of the T5 indexing represents a non-uniform distribution with the barcode assignment probabilities: pi for i=1, 2, …, n, while (b) the probabilities are uniform in the second stage of i5+i7 indexing: qj = 1/m for j=1, 2, …, m. The assumptions (a) and (b) give the expected number of cells with a combination of the barcodes (i,j) as λij = Cpi/m, where C is the total number of cells used. Since the mean parameter λ is constant λij = λi over j (during the second indexing), m observations in each ith row of X can be used as m i.i.d. samples from a Poisson distribution with parameter λi. Note that we can only observe that the number of assigned cells k in is zero (k=0; no cells assigned to the barcode) or non-zero (k>0; singlet, doublet, or more). The probability of k=0 is f(k=0; λi) = e−λi in the Poisson distribution; therefore, λi was estimated by λ^i = −log zi/m where zi is the number of unobserved barcodes in the ith row of X. The zi can be the number of barcodes for which the number of reads xij was less than a threshold in the ith row. Given a barcode (i, *), the probability r = f(k≥2; λ^i) can be used as a risk index of doublets. We excluded cells with r > 0.2 and a unique read count greater than twice the median.

To correct Tn5 bias, the regions detected as peaks by MACS247 for all datasets were blacklisted, and fragments overlapping the regions were excluded.

Quantification. Unique fragments were counted for each gene. For the reference genes, protein-coding genes and their loci were obtained from EnsDb.Mmusculus.v79. For genes with variants, the longest one is used as a representative.

The region for counting fragments was set as follows: RNAPII and H3K27me3; from TSS+1 kbp to TES+1 kbp, H3K4me3 and Brg1; TSS±5 kbp, H3K27ac; gene body.

Dimensional reduction. Dimensional reduction and clustering were performed following Seurat (version 5.3.0)48. Batch effects were removed by Harmony22 using principal components (PCs). PCs for downstream analysis were set based on an elbow plot. For all datasets, the correlation coefficients between Harmony components 1 and read count per cell were nearly |1|, so the components were excluded for the following analysis. Clustering was performed with the Seurat functions FindNeighbors and FindClusters. In FindClusters(), a Leiden algorithm was used.

Cell type annotation. Based on marker genes used by He et al. 27 and Cao et al. 26 for cell type annotation in scRNA-seq datasets, the clusters in sci-mtChIL-seq were evaluated using scType49. The cell types of the clusters were identified with reference to scType scores.

Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV). To visualize the aggregated signals distribution, the BigWig files were created by deeptools bamCoverage (version 3.5.4)50 for fragments of each dataset with the option --normalizeUsing CPM, –centerReads, -binSize 100, and --smoothLength 1000. For H3K27me3 fragments, the following values were used: -binSize 1000 --smoothLength 10000.

Gene Ontology (GO) enrichment analysis. GO enrichment analysis for biological processing was performed with the R package clusterProfiler (version 4.6.2)51 and org.Mm.eg.db.

Pseudotime analysis. The trajectory was inferred using the R package phateR (version 1.0.7)30 within the same principal component analysis space used for UMAP. Cells not involved in the biological process of interest, specifically non-muscle lineage cells, were excluded from the trajectory inference. Pseudotime was estimated using slingshot (version 2.6.0)52, based on the PHATE space. MyoD-negative cells were removed using a threshold estimated to distinguish between MyoD-positive and MyoD-negative samples.

The pseudotime was divided into 20 equally sized segments, referred to as PGs. PGs containing a small number of cells were merged with neighboring groups. For each PG, cells were aggregated, and fragment counts were obtained for each TF peak from ENCODE (MyoD: ENCFF814ERT, ENCFF138LQJ, ENCFF779ENE, ENCFF991ZUO; Myog: ENCFF277SLZ, ENCFF695DBU, ENCFF659JQU, ENCFF766TEE). These counts were used as estimates of TF binding levels.

To infer binding dynamics at each peak, binding levels were smoothed across PGs using a generalized additive model53, and the predicted values were scaled to the range [0, 1]. Peak clusters were identified via k-means clustering based on their dynamic profiles, with the number of clusters determined using silhouette analysis. Genes associated with promoter-proximal peaks (from −2 kbp to the TSS) were used for GO enrichment analysis.

Epigenome trajectory. Epigenomic regulation was inferred using the GeneTrajectory method33. Originally, this method estimates the sequential order of gene expression within a specific biological process, based on a low-dimensional representation of the Wasserstein distance between genes. The Wasserstein distance is computed pairwise between distributions of gene expression levels on a cell–cell graph, with the transportation cost defined by the shortest path. To reduce computational cost, a coarse-grained version of the cell–cell graph was used for the Wasserstein distance calculation.

In this study, we modified the processes of cell–cell graph construction and Wasserstein distance calculation to accommodate the sci-mtChIL-seq datasets. The cell–cell graph was constructed using the latent representation of RNAPII counts for binned coding regions (bin width=5 kbp), estimated by PeakVI54 to correct for batch effects and to estimate denoised counts. The count matrices for modalities other than RNAPII were also processed using PeakVI. A total of 1000 meta-cells were defined from the cell–cell graph using k-means clustering. For the coarse-graining step, denoised counts for all modalities were aggregated at the meta-cell level. Wasserstein distances were calculated among regions within the gene LOI to infer gene-specific epigenomic regulation.

For visualization of the results, a principal curve was inferred, and features were projected onto this curve55. The distributions of regulatory factors along the projected coordinates were estimated using the R package ggridges. The expression order was also determined based on these coordinates.

Bulk data analysis
Bulk RNA-seq (BRB-seq) data analysis. Read 1 (barcode read) was extracted by using UMI-tools with the following command “umi_tools extract -I read1.fastq --read2-in=read2.fastq --bc-pattern=NNNNNNNNNNCCCCCCCCC --read2-stdout ”. Adapter sequences and low-quality sequences were removed, and read lengths below 20 bp were discarded by using TrimGalore, and reads were mapped to the GRCm38 reference using HISAT2 (2.2.1)56. Read counts for each gene and each sample were obtained by summarizing the BAM file, which was produced by featureCounts (2.0.1)57.

Bulk ATAC-seq data analysis. Paired reads were mapped to the mm10 reference using Bowtie2. Alignments that were unpaired, discordant, or had fragment lengths exceeding 1000 bp were discarded. BAM files were created, sorted, and indexed by SAMtools. Bigwig files were created by the following command “bamCoverage --binSize 100 --centerReads --normalizeUsing CPM -b BAM.bam -o 100PE.CPM.bw”.

-Regarding the MyoD binding analyses, what does Fig. 3D show? The text first says a motif

We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. In the revised manuscript, we have removed
the original Fig. 3d and 3g, which presented trajectory-based lineage inference and transcription

and to focus the manuscript on experimentally supported results.
Nevertheless, we would like to clarify the original intent and interpretation of these analyses.
The goal was to infer the functional activity of MyoD during myogenesis by evaluating the
enrichment of MyoD-binding motifs across different pseudotime-defined cell clusters.
To quantify the enrichment levels of TF motifs around the MyoD bound sites, we applied
chromVAR, which is developed for ATAC-seq data to calculate a deviation score reflecting how
much motif accessibility deviates from a background model across datasets. In this way, the
deviation score serves as a quantitative proxy for transcription factor activity, allowing relative
comparisons of motif involvement across datasets.
In our case, MyoD bound sites were used as chromVAR inpu. A higher deviation score in the
myocytes indicated that these regions showed greater variability and were more specifically
engaged in those cells—consistent with MyoD's known role in muscle differentiation. The use of
chromVAR and deviation scores in this context is well established in single-cell chromatin
profiling, including scATAC-seq and ChIL-based methods.
That said, we agree with the reviewer that motif-level inference is not equivalent to direct
binding evidence, and that interpretation based on motif analysis should be supported by
functional validation. To avoid potential overinterpretation and streamline the manuscript, we
decided to omit this analysis and its associated figures from the revised version.

We appreciate the reviewer’s attention to the precision of terminology. In the revised manuscript,
we carefully avoided the use of the term lineage tracing, and instead described our approach using
trajectory inference or epigenomic trajectory to infer temporal regulatory order or differentiation
directionality based on chromatin states. Our method does not aim to trace heritable cell lineages
but rather captures state transitions inferred from chromatin dynamics. We agree that “lineage
tracing” is reserved for approaches that follow cell progeny using genetic labeling, and we have
ensured our revised text reflects this conceptual distinction.
